text:
Miles Thornton: need a quick gut check from folks before we lock v1 taxonomy. should “capacity exhaustion” be separate from “routing overload” or do we treat them as same bucket w/ contributing factors?

Miles Thornton: trying to keep it simple for ICs, but also want reporting to be meaningful. examples we saw last quarter:
- dedicated pool saturated (no GPUs) -> 5xx/timeouts
- hosted region had healthy GPUs but router kept shoving traffic to 1 AZ -> queueing
- sudden burst -> router qps spikes and sheds

Sean Gallagher: +1 on not overfitting, but these *feel* different operationally. capacity exhaustion is usually fleet/autoscaling/provisioning. routing overload is usually policy/routing/scheduler imbalance. mitigations differ.

Irene Choi: from infra POV, please separate. if you label everything “routing overload” we end up in the thread anyway bc it *looks* like overload externally, but root is “no capacity” / “can’t scale”.

Mina Haddad: disagree slightly: most pages start with “p95 latency up, 429/5xx” and we don’t know which it is. if taxonomy forces a choice too early, we’ll misclassify during response.

Rafael Mendes: maybe: category = what’s the *primary limiting factor at time of impact* (queueing in router vs no schedulable GPUs). and allow reclass after.

Aisha Bello: +1. we can make a rule: “pick best guess within 15 min” + “reclass in postmortem”. but still need two categories if SLAs differ.

Vanessa Ortiz: capacity exhaustion should include “autoscaler didn’t scale” and “fleet provisioning lag” and “quota hit”. routing overload is more like “router couldn’t spread load / policy regression / hot shard”.

Ethan Park: we also have control plane incidents where routing policies get stuck / stale weights, and then all traffic hits a subset. that’s not capacity per se. we need to attribute those to Platform.

Mina Haddad: ok but define “routing overload” carefully. overload can be *symptom* of capacity shortage.

Sean Gallagher: propose definitions:
1) Capacity exhaustion: demand > available compute capacity for target model/tier/region/pool (or capacity exists but cannot be brought online due to infra provisioning/autoscaling constraints). signals: GPU alloc fail, scheduler reports 0 available, autoscaler maxed, provisioning backlog.
2) Routing overload: router/policy/scheduler directs traffic such that a subset is overloaded while compatible capacity exists elsewhere OR routing layer itself becomes bottleneck (queueing at gateway/router, imbalance, hot partition). signals: uneven load across pools/AZs, healthy idle GPUs in other pools, routing error rate spikes, gateway saturation.

Sergio Costa: +1, also helps dashboards: “capacity” incidents correlate w utilization & provisioning metrics, “routing” correlate w imbalance metrics and policy deploys.

Dev Patel: from Support: we need category-to-playbook mapping. “capacity exhaustion” -> customers ask “do you need more GPUs? are we capped?”; “routing overload” -> “is this a bug/regression?” Messaging differs.

Mina Haddad: ok, but I want examples spelled out so oncall can pick:
- if dedicated pool is at max GPUs and queue grows -> capacity exhaustion
- if us-east has 60% idle but router keeps sending 90% to us-east-1a -> routing overload
- if gateway hits connection limit and drops streaming -> is that routing overload or edge/gateway?

Miles Thornton: gateway streaming is separate category in draft (“Edge/Gateway”). trying to keep “routing overload” scoped to smart-routing + scheduler distribution.

Irene Choi: for capacity exhaustion we should include “capacity exists but blocked” (quota, provisioning errors, node health checks failing). otherwise those get labeled “infra unknown”.

Sean Gallagher: agree. also clarify boundary with “fleet degradation” (hardware failures) vs “capacity exhaustion”. e.g. 30% GPUs offline due to bad driver rollout -> that’s arguably “fleet degradation” not pure exhaustion.

Aisha Bello: we can do: Category = primary. Contributing factors = secondary. So driver rollout causing lots of GPUs to drain -> category Fleet degradation, contributing factor leads to Capacity exhaustion symptoms.

Mina Haddad: that works. during incident, we can default to symptom-based category, then reclass once we confirm. but please don’t make people pick 2-3 things in the bot.

Rafael Mendes: policy idea:
- required during declare: Impacted surface + Customer tier + Region + Primary category (best guess)
- optional during declare: Contributing factor
- required by 24h/postmortem: confirm category + contributing factors + owning team

Sergio Costa: if we split categories, dashboards can show “% misclassified at declare vs postmortem” too. useful.

Ethan Park: ownership mapping if split:
- capacity exhaustion -> Infra/Fleet primary (with SRE)
- routing overload -> Platform/Routing primary
but we need note: capacity exhaustion can still be triggered by Platform (e.g., admission control disabled) -> contributing factor.

Miles Thornton: ok. question: what about “thundering herd / customer burst” that overwhelms? capacity vs routing?

Sean Gallagher: if demand legitimately exceeds provisioned capacity and autoscaler works as designed but hits max -> capacity exhaustion. if router fails to shed / enforce quotas and collapses -> routing overload or “rate limiting/admission control” category.

Irene Choi: +1. when a single customer burst consumes all capacity in shared pool, that’s “admission control/rate limiting misconfig” not fleet.

Mina Haddad: we have separate bucket for “quotas/rate limiting” already, right?

Miles Thornton: yes: “Traffic management (quotas/rate limit/admission control)”. so routing overload stays about distribution + routing infra bottlenecks.

Dev Patel: please make the definitions readable in one line for support + ICs. long definitions get ignored.

Miles Thornton: draft one-liners:
- Capacity exhaustion: “No schedulable compute for workload (pool/model/region/tier), due to demand > capacity or inability to scale/provision.”
- Routing overload: “Traffic distribution or routing layer bottleneck causes overload while compatible capacity exists elsewhere (imbalance/hotspot/policy).”

Sergio Costa: add “compatible capacity exists elsewhere” as key test. that makes it objective.

Aisha Bello: and remediation SLAs might differ: capacity exhaustion sev1 -> mitigate by shedding / failover / temporary extra capacity. routing overload sev1 -> mitigate by rollback policy / reweight / bypass smart routing.

Mina Haddad: ok I’m convinced on split. can we add an explicit note in doc: “If unsure, pick capacity exhaustion vs routing overload based on quickest observable signal: idle capacity elsewhere?”

Sean Gallagher: +1. heuristic:
- if global utilization high AND alloc failures -> capacity
- if utilization uneven OR idle capacity exists -> routing

Irene Choi: also add to capacity examples: “autoscaler maxed / provisioning backlog” and “regional GPU quota reached”. those show up a lot.

Rafael Mendes: action item: Miles update taxonomy doc with split + heuristic + examples, and I’ll update incident categorization policy to allow reclass.

Miles Thornton: done. will update v1 doc + bot help text. thanks all.

Sean Gallagher: :thumbsup:

Mina Haddad reacted with :+1:

Irene Choi reacted with :white_check_mark:

Sergio Costa: btw for dashboards, can we add a field “capacity_available_elsewhere=true/false/unknown” to support the heuristic?

Miles Thornton: optional field maybe, but trying to keep required set small. could be contributing factor / checkbox in postmortem.

Aisha Bello: +1 make it optional. we can compute some of it later from metrics (idle GPUs in other pools) but nice to capture human knowledge.

Dev Patel: please don’t add more fields to the declare flow. support already struggles to get IC to fill the basics.

Miles Thornton: ack. we’ll keep declare minimal; postmortem template can include “Was compatible capacity available elsewhere?” as a question.

Rafael Mendes: works. closing loop here.
